name: Email and Online Communication
objectives: Using a free email service's official website or app, create an email account with a professional address and a strong password and sign in to it, with a backup phone number or email added so you can get back in
Given a reason to write, write and send an email with a subject line, greeting, short message and sign-off, with all the parts present and the "To" address checked before sending
Given emails you received, reply, forward and attach a file, choosing Reply or Reply all correctly, with the file attached and the answer sent only to the people who need it
Given a suspicious email, identify its phishing warning signs and choose a safe next step, naming at least two signs and never clicking the link or paying
When writing to anyone online, write a polite, clear message that keeps private information out, with a greeting, no ALL CAPS, and no private numbers or passwords
Given a video call link, join the call and use the mute and camera buttons, joining on time and muting when not talking

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting a free email account
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a free email account and sign in to it.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free email service's official website or app, you will create an email account with a professional address and a strong password and sign in to it, with a backup phone number or email added so you can get back in.
An email address is like a home address for messages. It looks like name@gmail.com: your chosen name, the @ sign, then the company that runs it.
Free email services include Gmail from Google, Outlook.com from Microsoft and Yahoo Mail. To sign up, go to the company's own website or install its official app, and choose "Create account".
Pick an address that sounds professional, like your first and last name, because employers and doctors will see it. Choose a strong password you do not use anywhere else, and add a phone number or backup email so you can get back in if you forget it.
Step by step:
- Go to gmail.com, outlook.com or the official email app.
- Choose "Create account".
- Pick a professional address, like firstname.lastname.
- Make a long password you do not use anywhere else.
- Add a phone number or backup email for account recovery.
- Write your new address down and keep the password somewhere safe.
Words to know:
- Email address: your address for receiving messages, like name@gmail.com.
- Password: a secret word or phrase that lets only you into your account.
- Account recovery: the way to get back into your account if you forget your password, usually a code sent to your phone.
Try it now: Create a free email account (or open the one you already have). Sign out, then sign back in, so you know you can get in on your own.
You can now create a free email account with a professional address and sign in to it.

check.q: What does the @ sign do in an email address?
options: Separates your chosen name from the company that runs the email
check.why: An address is your chosen name, the @ sign, then the company, like name@gmail.com.

check.q: You are making an email account to apply for jobs. Which address would you choose?
options: Your first and last name, such as james.carter@...
check.why: Employers will see your address, so a name-based address sounds professional.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing a clear email
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write and send an email with a subject, greeting, short message and sign-off.
This lesson builds toward: Given a reason to write, you will write and send an email with a subject line, greeting, short message and sign-off, with all the parts present and the "To" address checked before sending.
A good email has five parts: who it goes to, a subject line, a greeting, a short message, and a sign-off with your name.
The subject line tells the reader what the email is about before they open it, for example "Question about my Tuesday appointment" or "Application for the cashier job".
Keep the message short: say why you are writing, what you need, and by when. Read it once before you press Send, and check the "To" address carefully, because you cannot take an email back once it is sent.
Step by step:
- Press Compose or New message.
- Type the person's address in the "To" box.
- Write a short subject line.
- Start with a greeting, like "Hello Ms. Lee,".
- Write two or three short sentences: why, what you need, by when.
- End with "Thank you," and your name.
- Read it once, check the address, then press Send.
Words to know:
- Subject line: a few words that tell the reader what the email is about.
- Compose: the button that starts a new email.
- Sign-off: the closing words, like "Thank you," followed by your name.
Try it now: Write and send an email to yourself or a family member with all five parts. Subject: "Practice email". Open it from the other side and see how it looks.
You can now write a clear email with a subject, greeting, short message and sign-off, and send it.

check.q: What should the short message part of an email say?
options: Why you are writing, what you need and by when
check.why: A short message says why you are writing, what you need and by when.

check.q: You are about to send an email to your doctor's office. What would you check first?
options: The "To" address, and read the email once
How many emails are in your inbox
Whether the subject is in ALL CAPS
check.why: You cannot take an email back, so check the address and read it before sending.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Replying, forwarding and attaching a file
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Reply to an email and send one with a file attached.
This lesson builds toward: Given emails you received, you will reply, forward and attach a file, choosing Reply or Reply all correctly, with the file attached and the answer sent only to the people who need it.
Reply sends your answer only to the person who wrote to you. Reply all sends it to everyone on the message, so use it only when everyone needs your answer. Forward sends the email on to someone new.
An attachment is a file you send with an email, like a photo, a résumé or a form. Look for the paper clip icon. Choose the file from your phone or computer, wait until it finishes loading, then send.
Only open attachments you were expecting from people you know. Files from strangers can carry harmful programs.
Step by step:
- Open the email you want to answer.
- Press Reply (not Reply all, unless everyone needs it).
- Write your answer and press Send.
- To attach a file: in a new email, press the paper clip icon.
- Choose the photo or document and wait for it to load.
- Mention the file in your message, then press Send.
Words to know:
- Reply all: answers everyone who got the email, not just the sender.
- Forward: sends an email you got on to someone else.
- Attachment: a file sent along with an email.
Try it now: Reply to the practice email from Lesson 2. Then write a new email to yourself, attach one photo or document, and send it. Open it and check that the file arrived.
You can now reply to an email, forward one, and send a file as an attachment.

options: A file you send with an email, like a photo or form
check.why: An attachment is a file sent along with an email.

check.q: You attached your résumé, but it is still loading. What would you do?
options: Wait until it finishes loading, then send
check.why: Wait until the file finishes loading, or it may not go with the email.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Staying safe and talking online

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Spotting phishing and scam emails
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an email for warning signs before you click anything.
This lesson builds toward: Given a suspicious email, you will identify its phishing warning signs and choose a safe next step, naming at least two signs and never clicking the link or paying.
Phishing is a fake message that pretends to be from a bank, a store, a delivery company or a government office, to trick you into clicking a link or giving private information.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) lists common signs: the message pretends to be from an organization you know, says there is a problem or a prize, pushes you to act right away, and asks you to pay in an unusual way such as gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency.
Also look at the sender's real address: "support@amaz0n-help.win" is not Amazon. When in doubt, do not click. Go to the company's website yourself, or call a number you already know is real. In the United States you can report scams at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Look at the sender's full address, not just the name.
- Ask: Does it pretend to be someone I know? Is there a problem or a prize? Am I being rushed? Do they want gift cards or a wire transfer?
- If yes to any, do not click links or open files.
- Check by going to the real website yourself or calling a known number.
- Delete it or mark it as spam. In the US, report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Phishing: a fake message made to trick you into clicking a link or giving private information.
- Spam: unwanted junk email.
- FTC: the Federal Trade Commission, the US government office that handles scam reports.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam
- FTC: Report fraud
Try it now: Open your spam or junk folder and pick one message. Find at least two warning signs in it. Do not click any links. Then delete it.
You can now check an email for the four warning signs and the sender's real address before you click.

options: A way to attach large files
A fake message pretending to be from a company or office to trick you
check.why: Phishing pretends to be from a trusted name to get you to click or share information.

check.q: An email says you won a prize and must pay a small fee with gift cards today. What would you do?
options: Do not click or pay; it shows scam signs
Forward it to friends so they can win too
check.why: A prize, pressure to act now and gift-card payment are all scam signs the FTC lists.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Good manners online
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write a polite, clear message that gets a good response.
This lesson builds toward: When writing to anyone online, you will write a polite, clear message that keeps private information out, with a greeting, no ALL CAPS, and no private numbers or passwords.
People cannot hear your voice in a written message, so words can sound harsher than you mean. ALL CAPITAL LETTERS reads like shouting.
Be polite and short. Use a greeting and "please" and "thank you". Answer important emails within a day or two, even if only to say "I got this and will reply by Friday".
Before you send a message when you are upset, wait a little and read it again. Do not put private information like your Social Security number, bank numbers or passwords in an email or chat message.
Step by step:
- Start with a greeting.
- Say what you need in short sentences.
- Use normal capital letters, not ALL CAPS.
- Say please and thank you.
- If you are upset, wait and reread before sending.
- Leave out private numbers and passwords.
Words to know:
- Netiquette: good manners for messages and posts online.
- ALL CAPS: writing in all capital letters, which reads like shouting.
Try it now: Write a short, polite email to a landlord, school, clinic or employer (you do not have to send it) asking a question. Read it out loud: does it sound friendly and clear?
You can now write a polite, clear message and avoid habits that cause trouble online.

check.q: Why can written words sound harsher than you mean?
options: People cannot hear your voice in a written message
check.why: Without your voice, the reader only has your words to go by.

check.q: An important email arrives but you need a few days to answer. What would you do?
options: Ignore it until you are ready
Reply within a day or two to say when you will answer
check.why: A short reply such as "I got this and will reply by Friday" is good manners.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Joining a video call
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Join a video call from a link and use mute and camera buttons.
This lesson builds toward: Given a video call link, you will join the call and use the mute and camera buttons, joining on time and muting when not talking.
Many doctors, employers, schools and families use video calls. Common free ones are Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and FaceTime on Apple devices. Usually someone sends you a link by email or text.
Tap or click the link a few minutes early. On a phone it may ask you to install the app from the official app store. When asked, allow the microphone and camera.
Learn two buttons: the microphone (mute and unmute) and the camera (on and off). Sit facing a light, in a quiet place, and mute yourself when you are not talking.
Step by step:
- Find the link in the email or text from someone you know.
- Join five minutes early.
- If asked, install the official app or open it in the browser.
- Allow the microphone and camera.
- Find the mute and camera buttons.
- Face a light, find a quiet spot, and mute when not talking.
- Press Leave or the red button to hang up.
Words to know:
- Video call: a call where you can see and hear each other on a screen.
- Mute: turns your microphone off so others cannot hear you.
- Meeting link: a web address that takes you straight into a video call.
Try it now: Final task practice: ask a friend or family member to send you a video call link (or start a Google Meet or Zoom call yourself). Join it, mute and unmute, turn the camera off and on, then leave the call.
You can now join a video call from a link, use the mute and camera buttons, and leave the call.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear email The subject line, greeting, message or sign-off is missing. A subject line, a greeting, two or three short sentences and a sign-off with your name. The subject line says exactly what the email is about and the message says what you need and by when. Attachment No file is attached, or it did not finish loading. One photo or document is attached and arrives with the email. The file has a clear name and the email mentions what is attached. Reply No reply was sent, or Reply all was used when only one person needed it. A reply was sent to the right person. The reply is polite and answers every question in the email. Polite and private The email is in ALL CAPS, sounds rude, or contains private numbers or passwords. The email is polite, uses normal capital letters and has no private information. Uses please and thank you and reads well on the first try. Phishing signs Fewer than two warning signs, or a sign is wrong. Two correct warning signs to look for before clicking any link. Also says what to do instead of clicking and where to report a scam. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How do you usually join a video call?
options: By calling a phone number from a pop-up
By tapping or clicking a link someone sent you
By sending an email to the app
check.why: Usually someone sends you a link by email or text, and you tap it to join.

check.q: Your video interview starts at 10:00. What would you do?
options: Join from a noisy room with the light behind you
Keep your microphone on the whole time while others talk
Join a few minutes early in a quiet place, facing a light
check.why: Joining early lets you install the app and allow the microphone and camera in time.
